deep.reconstruction:
The page is not a derivation. It is a computed ephemeris table: the April page of a month-by-month table of star-reduction quantities that runs from 'März' (fol. 135) through 'April' (this page) to 'May' (fol. 137). The header '91 +' is the running day-of-year of the first row (31+28+31 = 90, so April 1 is day 91; March is headed 60 and May 121). The first row of each month repeats the last row of the previous month: March 32 = April 1 and April 31 = May 1.

The columns can be identified from their own numbers. Write λ for the Sun's longitude.

Col. 1 (0.2518 to 0.3337): the fraction of the year τ. It rises by 0.0819 over 30 rows, i.e. 0.002730 per row. That equals 1/366.24, not 1/365.25. So the rows are probably spaced one sidereal day apart (366.24 sidereal days to the year), for example successive instants of 0h sidereal time (my inference). Three facts support this. March and May have 32 rows. The tabulated daily solar motion (58'54'' falling to 58'00'') is about 10'' smaller than the true motion per mean solar day. That gap matches the factor 0.99727 between sidereal and solar days.

Col. 4: the Sun's true longitude λ in degrees, minutes and seconds, from 12°34'22'' to 41°46'45''.

Col. 3: Bessel's B, solar part only. It fits B = −0.43'' cos 2λ to the last digit. For example, at λ = 26°16', −0.43·cos 52.5° = −0.26.

Col. 2: Bessel's A, solar part only. The difference A − τ fits ≈ −0.0199·sin 2λ: −0.0085 on Apr 1, −0.0198 on May 1, +0.0117 on Mar 1, ~0 at the equinox. Multiplied by the annual precession (~50.2''), this amplitude corresponds to a solar nutation in longitude of about 1.0''. In both A and B the lunar (node) terms are absent: they would have to vanish at once in sin Ω and cos Ω, which is impossible. So this is a table of the solar parts only; the lunar parts must be added from elsewhere (my inference).

Cols. 6 and 7: Bessel's aberration day numbers C = −κ cos ε cos λ and D = −κ sin λ. Fits give κ cos ε ≈ 18.91 and κ ≈ 20.60–20.61, so ε ≈ 23°28'.

Col. 5: Bessel's i = C tan ε = −κ sin ε cos λ = −8.21 cos λ. (Note that tan ε ≈ 0.4342, numerically almost equal to log10 e.)

Cols. 8 and 9: the polar form of the aberration numbers, C = h sin H and D = h cos H. Col. 8 is H in degrees and minutes (for example 252.7 means 252°07'). Col. 9 is log10 h. Check for Apr 1: atan2(−18.45, −4.49) = 256.32° = 256°19'–20' and log10 √(18.45² + 4.49²) = 1.2785. Check for Apr 5: H = 252°07', log h = 1.2799.

Thus the table supplies, for each sidereal day, the Besselian day numbers A, B, C, D in the form (A, B, i, h, H). These are used to reduce mean star places to apparent places: Δα = Aa + Bb + Cc + Dd, with the Cc + Dd part computed via h sin(H + α) etc. and the i tan-term in declination.
errors: Apr 19, Sun's longitude written 30°9'29''. The day-to-day differences around it are 58'22'', then 58'30'', then 58'08''; they should decrease smoothly by about 1–2'' per day. The value should be about 30°9'19'' (a 10'' slip). The derived columns are insensitive at this level and agree with either value.

Apr 31 (= May 1), Sun's longitude written 41°46'45''. The last difference then becomes 57'48'' against the expected ~57'58''. The May page repeats the same row as 41°46'55'', which is the smooth value; the April entry is a 10'' copying slip.

No errors found in the A, B, i, C, D, H, log h columns at the points checked (Apr 1, 5, 15, 17, 31). The aberration constant implied by the table, κ ≈ 20.6'', is larger than the values in standard use at the time (Delambre/Bessel 20.25''; Struve 1843 20.445''). This is not an arithmetic error but a notable choice of constant, or else the columns include a factor I have not identified.

results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers A, B (solar nutation terms)
results.usually_credited_to: F. W. Bessel (Tabulae Regiomontanae, 1830; partly Fundamenta Astronomiae, 1818)

results.modern_name: Besselian day numbers C, D and i

results.what: Polar form C = h sin H, D = h cos H, tabulated as H and log h
results.modern_name: Bessel's h, H form of the aberration day numbers

results.what: Rows spaced by sidereal days (τ increment 1/366.24, 32 rows in March and May)

deep.surprise_reason: This is a routine computed reduction table, with no derivation. It is in Bessel's day-number format (A, B, i, h, H). It would be mildly interesting only if the folio really predates Bessel's 1830 Tabulae Regiomontanae, which the bundle name alone does not establish. The slightly unusual constants (κ ≈ 20.6'', a solar nutation of ≈ 0.43''/1.0'') are also mildly interesting.

transcription_corrections: The machine transcription matches the image; the slips noted under errors are Gauss's own, not transcription errors. Apr 19 longitude reads '30.9.29' (underlined in the MS) and should be about 30.9.19; Apr 31 reads '41.46.45' where the May page gives the correct 41.46.55.
Column 8 entries such as '252.7', '251.4', '250.1' are degrees.minutes, i.e. 252°07', 251°04', 250°01'.
The header '91 +' is the day-of-year of April 1 (matching '60' on March and '121' on May).
